newsitem.title: JAPAN: Investors await individual Japanese stock options.
newsitem.headline: Investors await individual Japanese stock options.

text.p: Bourses in Tokyo and Osaka will start trading individual stock options later this month as part of a drive to liberalise Japan's financial markets and catch up with other global financial centres.

The launch of the new derivatives on July 18 is being eagerly awaited by institutional investors who see them as useful tools to hedge investment risks and bring in profits. Market participants hope they will help put an end to a long-running slump in stock trading volumes in Japan.
"Trading equity options is attractive because they will increase profit opportunities," said Hitoshi Morimura, chief portfolio manager at the stocks department of Meiji Life Insurance Co.

"In the past, we could take profits only when prices rose (by unloading share holdings), but the equity options will make it possible for us to go short first and take profits when prices decline," he said.
Options, typically used to hedge against losses due to price fluctuations, allow a holder to buy or sell a specified amount of shares at an agreed price during a set time period.

By making an option contract for the right to sell stocks at a fixed price, investors can reduce risks in investing in cash stocks, because they can exercise the option contract in the event of a sharp decline in cash stock prices.

While Japan introduced stock index futures and options in the late 1980s, it has taken a cautious approach to derivatives on individual stocks, pushing the lucrative business offshore to less regulated markets, where brokers are able to trade options or warrants based on Japanese stocks if they wish.
The Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) and the Osaka Securities Exchange (OSE) will initially each list 20 issues eligible for options trade. The maximum option period will initially be set at eight months.
The OSE said last month it was also considering listing futures and options covering high-technology, consumer and financial indices.
"Japanese equity options trading has finally started to catch up with the United States and Britain," Morimura said. "But it is just the beginning and the number of issues is still small."

A Ministry of Finance official said Japan would need to increase the number of issues eligible for options trade and extend the maximum option period to help institutional investors trade them more actively.

Japan's bourses are seeking to make themselves more attractive to investors ahead of planned "Big Bang" reforms, through which Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has said he aims to make Japanese financial markets "free, fair and global".
As part of that push, Japan is expected to introduce over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives next year, and to lift controls on stockbroking fees by the end of 1999.

Nicholas Waltner, co-head of Japanese equity derivatives at Salomon Brothers in Tokyo, said trade in Japan's equities derivatives would become as active as that in Europe and the United States as a result of the listing of equity options, the planned introduction of OTC stock derivatives, and the deregulation of stock commissions.
Waltner said: "We expect Japan's equity derivatives market to be commensurate with its status as the world's second-largest equity market."
